lessons.title: Describing your home
lessons.goal: Say where you live and describe your rooms.

tip.title: il y a & pièce vs chambre
tip.body: il y a means there is / there are, for one thing or many: Il y a trois pièces. In the negative, un/une/des become de (d' before a vowel): Il n'y a pas d'ascenseur. In everyday speech il y a often sounds like 'ya'. Careful with false friends: une pièce is any room, une chambre is a bedroom, and un appartement is a flat. Floors: au troisième étage = on the third floor (counted above the ground floor).

lessons.title: Renting a flat
lessons.goal: Ask about rent, charges and moving in.

tip.title: Flat sizes & asking questions
tip.body: French flats are counted by main rooms: a T2 or F2 (un deux-pièces) has a living room and one bedroom; kitchen and bathroom don't count. Un studio is a one-room flat. Rent is le loyer; les charges are the service charges (building costs, sometimes heating), and la caution or le dépôt de garantie is the deposit. Ask questions three ways: Le loyer, c'est combien ? (intonation), Est-ce que les charges sont comprises ? or Les charges sont-elles comprises ? (more formal). Meublé = furnished.

lessons.title: Neighbours & house rules
lessons.goal: Introduce yourself to a neighbour and ask about the building.

tip.title: Good neighbours
tip.body: In French blocks of flats (un immeuble) it's polite to say Bonjour to neighbours on the stairs, and before a party many people put a note in the hall to warn them about the noise. Some buildings have a gardien or gardienne (traditionally la concierge) who looks after the building and the post. Rubbish is sorted: les poubelles are the bins, and yellow-lidded bins are often for recycling — check the local rules. Say voisin with a nasal 'in' at the end; voisine (female) has no nasal: voi-zine.

phrases.t: N'hésitez pas à frapper à ma porte.

lessons.title: Where things are & adjective position
lessons.goal: Say where things are and describe them with adjectives.

tip.title: Prepositions of place & BANGS
tip.body: sur (on), sous (under), dans (in), devant (in front of), derrière (behind), entre (between). Prepositions ending in de merge with le/les: à côté du lit, en face des fenêtres (de + le = du, de + les = des). Most adjectives come after the noun: une cuisine moderne. But short, common adjectives of Beauty, Age, Number, Goodness and Size (BANGS) come before: une jolie chambre, un vieux canapé, un grand salon, un petit jardin. Before a vowel, beau, nouveau and vieux become bel, nouvel, vieil: un vieil immeuble, un nouvel appartement — same sound as the feminine.

story.title: A new start
story.intro: Karim bumps into his friend Inès, who has just moved out of central Lyon.

lines.name: Karim
lines.t: Inès ! Ça fait longtemps ! Tu habites toujours près de la place Bellecour ?
lines.n: Inès! It's been ages! Do you still live near Place Bellecour?

lines.name: Inès
lines.t: Non, j'ai déménagé le mois dernier. Maintenant, j'habite à Villeurbanne.
lines.n: No, I moved last month. Now I live in Villeurbanne.

lines.name: Karim
lines.t: Ah bon ? Pourquoi ? Tu aimais bien ton quartier !
lines.n: Really? Why? You liked your neighbourhood!

lines.name: Inès
lines.t: Oui, mais l'appartement était un studio au cinquième sans ascenseur. C'était trop petit et trop cher.
lines.n: Yes, but the flat was a studio on the fifth floor with no lift. It was too small and too expensive.

lines.name: Karim
lines.t: Et le nouveau, il est comment ?
lines.n: And what's the new one like?

lines.name: Inès
lines.t: C'est un trois-pièces au rez-de-chaussée. Et maintenant, on a un jardin !
lines.n: It's a two-bedroom flat on the ground floor. And now we have a garden!

lines.name: Karim
lines.t: On ? Tu n'habites pas seule ?
lines.n: We? You don't live alone?

lines.name: Inès
lines.t: Non, avec mon copain et notre chien. Le chien adore le jardin !

lines.name: Karim
lines.t: Super ! Et c'est loin du centre ?

lines.t: Non, vingt minutes en métro. Il faut venir pendre la crémaillère samedi !

culture.title: Floors and room counts
culture.body: In France, Belgium and Switzerland the ground floor is le rez-de-chaussée (often written RDC) and le premier étage is the floor above — like British, not American, English. Room counts differ: in France a T3 has three main rooms (living room plus two bedrooms). In Switzerland ads often count half rooms, e.g. 3,5 pièces. In Québec, flats are described like un trois et demi (3 ½): kitchen, living room and bedroom, with the bathroom counted as the half. Many Québec leases traditionally end on 1 July, so the province has a big moving day then.
